Initialize a StGit stack on a branch.

Initializing a branch with a StGit stack commits initial, empty stack state for the
branch to the repository. Theses stack metadata commits are tracked by the
`refs/stacks/<branch>` reference. Updated stack state is committed by each StGit command
that modifies the stack. StGit users do not have to do anything with the
`refs/stacks/<branch>` ref directly.

Some StGit commands, such as `stg new` and `stg uncommit`, will automatically initialize
the stack, so it is often not necessary to explicitly initialize the stack on a branch.
Also, branches created with `stg branch --create` are automatically initialized.

The branch must already exist and point to a commit before initializing a StGit stack.

StGit stack metadata can be deinitialized from a branch using `stg branch --cleanup`.
See 'stg branch' for more details.

Usage: stg init [OPTIONS]

Options:
  -b, --branch <branch>
          Use <branch> instead of current branch

      --color <when>
          Specify when to colorize the output.
          
          `auto` (the default) enables colored output only when outputting to a terminal
          or TTY. The `NO_COLOR` environment variable is respected.
          
          `always` and `never` unconditionlly enable/disable colored output,
          respectively.
          
          `ansi` forces color to be output using ANSI escape sequences, even in a
          Windows console.

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
Create a new, empty patch on the current stack. The new patch is created on top of the
currently applied patches, and is made the new top of the stack. Uncommitted changes in
the work tree are not included in the patch -- that is handled by stg-refresh.

The given patch name must be unique in the stack. If no name is given, one is generated
from the first line of the patch's commit message.

Patch names follow the rules for Git references with the additional constraint that
patch names may not contain the '/' character. See git-check-ref-format(1) for details.

Patch names may start with a leading '-'. When specifying such a patch name on the
command line, the leading '-' may be escaped with a single backslash as in
'\-patch-name' to disambiguate the patch name from command line options.

An editor will be launched to edit the commit message to be used for the patch, unless
the '--message' flag already specified one. The 'patchdescr.tmpl' template file (if
available) is used to pre-fill the editor.

Usage: stg new [OPTIONS] [patchname] [-- <path>...]
       stg new [OPTIONS] [--name <patchname>] [-- <path>...]

Arguments:
  [patchname]
          Name for new patch

  [path]...
          Refresh files matching path(s). Specifying paths implies '--refresh'. Using
          '--refresh' without any paths will target all modified files.

Options:
  -n, --name <name>
          Alternative to the [patchname] argument for specifying the name of the new
          patch. This option allows the patch name to start with an unescaped leading
          '-'.

      --color <when>
          Specify when to colorize the output.
          
          `auto` (the default) enables colored output only when outputting to a terminal
          or TTY. The `NO_COLOR` environment variable is respected.
          
          `always` and `never` unconditionlly enable/disable colored output,
          respectively.
          
          `ansi` forces color to be output using ANSI escape sequences, even in a
          Windows console.

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

Refresh Options:
  -r, --refresh
          Refresh the new patch with changes from work tree. New patches are empty by
          default, but with this option the new patch will capture outstanding changes
          in the work tree as if 'stg refresh' was run. Use '--index' to refresh from
          the index instead of the work tree.

  -i, --index
          Instead of refreshing the patch with the current contents of the worktree, use
          the current contents of the index.

  -F, --force
          Force refresh with staged and unstaged changes.
          
          By default, if there are staged changes in the index along with unstaged
          changes in the work tree, the command will abort. This option forces the
          command to proceed using both the staged and unstaged changes.

      --submodules
          Include submodules in patch content

      --no-submodules
          Exclude submodules in patch content

Patch Edit Options:
  -e, --edit
          Invoke editor for patch description

  -d, --diff
          Show diff when editing patch description

  -m, --message <message>
          Use message instead of invoking the editor

  -f, --file <path>
          Use the contents of file instead of invoking the editor. Use "-" to read from
          stdin.

      --no-verify
          Disable commit-msg hook

  -s, --signoff[=<value>]
          Add "Signed-off-by" message trailer.
          
          The value is optional and defaults to the committer name and email. This
          option may be provided multiple times.

      --ack[=<value>]
          Add "Acked-by" message trailer.
          
          The value is optional and defaults to the committer's name and email. This
          option may be provided multiple times.

      --review[=<value>]
          Add "Reviewed-by" message trailer.
          
          The value is optional and defaults to the committer's name and email. This
          option may be provided multiple times.

      --author <name-and-email>
          Set the author "name <email>"

      --authname <name>
          Set the author name

      --authemail <email>
          Set the author email

      --authdate <date>
          Set the date the patch was authored.
          
          Use "now" to use the current time and date.

      --committer-date-is-author-date
          Instead of using the current time as the committer date, use the author date

Show all the patches in the series, or just those in the given range, ordered from
bottom to top.

The topmost applied patch is prefixed with '>'. All other applied patches are prefixed
with '+'. Unapplied patches are prefixed with '-' and hidden patches with '!'.

The --reverse option may be used to reverse the order in which patches are displayed.
The reversed order is more stack-like, with the base of the stack appearing at the
bottom of of the display.

Empty patches are prefixed with a '*' when the --empty option is used.

Usage: stg series [OPTIONS] [-A] [-U] [-H]
       stg series [OPTIONS] --all
       stg series [OPTIONS] --short
       stg series [OPTIONS] [patch]...

Arguments:
  [patch]...
          Patches to display

Options:
  -b, --branch <branch>
          Use <branch> instead of current branch

      --color <when>
          Specify when to colorize the output.
          
          `auto` (the default) enables colored output only when outputting to a terminal
          or TTY. The `NO_COLOR` environment variable is respected.
          
          `always` and `never` unconditionlly enable/disable colored output,
          respectively.
          
          `ansi` forces color to be output using ANSI escape sequences, even in a
          Windows console.

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

Select Options:
  -a, --all
          Select all patches, including hidden patches

  -s, --short[=<n>]
          Select <n> patches around the topmost patch only

  -A, --applied
          Select the applied patches only

  -U, --unapplied
          Select the unapplied patches only

  -H, --hidden
          Select the hidden patches only

  -m, --missing <branch>
          Select patches in <branch> not present in current branch

Display Options:
      --author
          Display author name for each patch

  -c, --count
          Display the number of selected patches and exit

  -i, --commit-id[=<length>]
          Display the commit id for each patch.
          
          The optional length indicates how many prefix characters of the commit id to
          display. The default is "full", which displays the full commit id, but may
          alternatively be specified as a positive integer greater than or equal to 4.

          Display short description for each patch

  -e, --empty
          Before the '+', '>', '-', and '!' prefixes, print a column that contains
          either '0' (for empty patches) or a space (for non-empty patches).

  -P, --no-prefix
          Do not display the patch status prefix

  -I, --indices
          Display absolute patch indicies

  -O, --offsets
          Display relative offsets from topmost patch or from the stack base if no
          patches are applied.

  -r, --reverse
          Display patches in reverse order.

          printed in order from bottom to top; i.e. the first patch in the stack is
          printed first and the last patch is printed last. Thus with the default

          display, which may be more intuitive.

this kind of situation:

to reset the stack/branch to any previous stack state.

2. Use `stg repair`. This will repair the StGit stack metadata to accommodate the
modifications to the branch made by the git commands. Specifically, it will do the
following:

- If regular git commits were made on top of the stack of StGit patches (i.e. by using
plain `git commit`), `stg repair` will convert those commits to StGit patches,
preserving their content.

they are no longer reachable. An alternative when this is not the desired behavior is to
use `stg undo` to first get rid of the offending merge and then run `stg repair` again.

branch head. If, for example, git-reset(1) was used to move the head, some applied
patches may no longer be reachable and some unapplied patches may have become reachable.

stg-init(1)
===========

NAME
----
stg-init - Initialize a StGit stack on a branch

SYNOPSIS
--------
[verse]
'stg init' [OPTIONS]

DESCRIPTION
-----------

Initialize a StGit stack on a branch.

Initializing a branch with a StGit stack commits initial, empty stack state for
the branch to the repository. Theses stack metadata commits are tracked by the
`refs/stacks/<branch>` reference. Updated stack state is committed by each
StGit command that modifies the stack. StGit users do not have to do anything
with the `refs/stacks/<branch>` ref directly.

Some StGit commands, such as `stg new` and `stg uncommit`, will automatically
initialize the stack, so it is often not necessary to explicitly initialize the
stack on a branch. Also, branches created with `stg branch --create` are
automatically initialized.

The branch must already exist and point to a commit before initializing a StGit stack.

StGit stack metadata can be deinitialized from a branch using `stg branch
--cleanup`. See linkstg:branch[] for more details.

OPTIONS
-------
-b <branch>::
--branch=<branch>::
    Use <branch> instead of current branch

StGit
</output>

// Internal
use crate::builder::Command;

use crate::output::Usage;

/// Writes the parser help to the wrapped stream.
pub(crate) fn write_help(writer: &mut StyledStr, cmd: &Command, usage: &Usage<'_>, use_long: bool) {
    debug!("write_help");

    if let Some(h) = cmd.get_override_help() {
        writer.push_styled(h);
    } else {
        #[cfg(feature = "help")]
        {
            use super::AutoHelp;
            use super::HelpTemplate;
            if let Some(tmpl) = cmd.get_help_template() {
                HelpTemplate::new(writer, cmd, usage, use_long)

            } else {

            }
        }

        #[cfg(not(feature = "help"))]
        {
            debug!("write_help: no help, `Command::override_help` and `help` is missing");
        }
    }

    // Remove any lines from unused sections
    writer.trim_start_lines();
    // Remove any whitespace caused by book keeping
    writer.trim_end();
    // Ensure there is still a trailing newline
    writer.push_str("\n");
}

/// Basic template methods
impl HelpTemplate<'_, '_> {
    /// Writes binary name of a Parser Object to the wrapped stream.
    fn write_display_name(&mut self) {
        debug!("HelpTemplate::write_display_name");

        let display_name = wrap(
            &self
                .cmd
                .get_display_name()
                .unwrap_or_else(|| self.cmd.get_name())
                .replace("{n}", "\n"),
            self.term_w,
        );
        self.writer.push_string(display_name);
    }

    /// Writes binary name of a Parser Object to the wrapped stream.
    #[cfg(not(feature = "unstable-v5"))]
    fn write_bin_name(&mut self) {
        debug!("HelpTemplate::write_bin_name");

        let bin_name = if let Some(bn) = self.cmd.get_bin_name() {
            if bn.contains(' ') {
                // In case we're dealing with subcommands i.e. git mv is translated to git-mv
                bn.replace(' ', "-")
            } else {
                wrap(&self.cmd.get_name().replace("{n}", "\n"), self.term_w)
            }
        } else {
            wrap(&self.cmd.get_name().replace("{n}", "\n"), self.term_w)
        };
        self.writer.push_string(bin_name);
    }

    fn write_version(&mut self) {
        let version = self
            .cmd
            .get_version()
            .or_else(|| self.cmd.get_long_version());
        if let Some(output) = version {
            self.writer.push_string(wrap(output, self.term_w));
        }
    }

    fn write_author(&mut self, before_new_line: bool, after_new_line: bool) {
        if let Some(author) = self.cmd.get_author() {
            if before_new_line {
                self.writer.push_str("\n");
            }
            self.writer.push_string(wrap(author, self.term_w));
            if after_new_line {
                self.writer.push_str("\n");
            }
        }
    }

    fn write_about(&mut self, before_new_line: bool, after_new_line: bool) {
        let about = if self.use_long {
            self.cmd.get_long_about().or_else(|| self.cmd.get_about())
        } else {
            self.cmd.get_about()
        };
        if let Some(output) = about {
            if before_new_line {
                self.writer.push_str("\n");
            }
            let mut output = output.clone();
            output.replace_newline_var();
            output.wrap(self.term_w);
            self.writer.push_styled(&output);
            if after_new_line {
                self.writer.push_str("\n");
            }
        }
    }

    fn write_before_help(&mut self) {
        debug!("HelpTemplate::write_before_help");
        let before_help = if self.use_long {
            self.cmd

            self.cmd.get_before_help()

        if let Some(output) = before_help {
            let mut output = output.clone();
            output.replace_newline_var();
            output.wrap(self.term_w);
            self.writer.push_styled(&output);
            self.writer.push_str("\n\n");
        }
    }

    fn write_after_help(&mut self) {
        debug!("HelpTemplate::write_after_help");
        let after_help = if self.use_long {
            self.cmd

            output.replace_newline_var();
            output.wrap(self.term_w);
            self.writer.push_styled(&output);

    /// Sorts arguments by length and display order and write their help to the wrapped stream.
    fn write_args(&mut self, args: &[&Arg], _category: &str, sort_key: ArgSortKey) {
        debug!("HelpTemplate::write_args {_category}");
        // The shortest an arg can legally be is 2 (i.e. '-x')
        let mut longest = 2;
        let mut ord_v = BTreeMap::new();

        // Determine the longest
        for &arg in args.iter().filter(|arg| {
            // If it's NextLineHelp we don't care to compute how long it is because it may be
            // NextLineHelp on purpose simply *because* it's so long and would throw off all other
            // args alignment
            should_show_arg(self.use_long, arg)
        }) {
            let width = display_width(&arg.to_string());
            let actual_width = if arg.get_long().is_some() {
                width + SHORT_SIZE
            } else {
                width
            };
            longest = longest.max(actual_width);
            debug!(
                "HelpTemplate::write_args: arg={:?} longest={}",
                arg.get_id(),
                longest
            );

            let key = (sort_key)(arg);
            ord_v.insert(key, arg);
        }

        let next_line_help = self.will_args_wrap(args, longest);

        for (i, (_, arg)) in ord_v.iter().enumerate() {
            if i != 0 {
                self.writer.push_str("\n");
                if next_line_help && self.use_long {
                    self.writer.push_str("\n");
                }
            }
            self.write_arg(arg, next_line_help, longest);
        }
    }

/// # Examples

/// **Note:** When the `unicode` Cargo feature is disabled, all characters are presumed to take up

///
/// An example of a decomposed character is “é”, which can be decomposed into: “e” followed by a
/// combining acute accent: “◌́”.  Without the `unicode` Cargo feature, every `char` has a width of
/// 1. This includes the combining accent:
///
/// ## Emojis and CJK Characters
///
/// Characters such as emojis and [CJK characters] used in the
/// Chinese, Japanese, and Korean languages are seen as double-width,
/// even if the `unicode-width` feature is disabled:
///
/// # Limitations
///
/// The displayed width of a string cannot always be computed from the
/// string alone. This is because the width depends on the rendering
/// engine used. This is particularly visible with [emoji modifier
/// sequences] where a base emoji is modified with, e.g., skin tone or
/// hair color modifiers. It is up to the rendering engine to detect
/// this and to produce a suitable emoji.
///
/// A simple example is “❤️”, which consists of “❤” (U+2764: Black
/// Heart Symbol) followed by U+FE0F (Variation Selector-16). By
/// itself, “❤” is a black heart, but if you follow it with the
/// variant selector, you may get a wider red heart.
///
/// A more complex example would be “👨‍🦰” which should depict a man
/// with red hair. Here the computed width is too large — and the
/// width differs depending on the use of the `unicode-width` feature:
///
/// This happens because the grapheme consists of three code points:
/// “👨” (U+1F468: Man), Zero Width Joiner (U+200D), and “🦰”
/// (U+1F9B0: Red Hair). You can see them above in the test. With
/// `unicode-width` enabled, the ZWJ is correctly seen as having zero
/// width, without it is counted as a double-width character.
///
/// ## Terminal Support
///
/// Modern browsers typically do a great job at combining characters
/// as shown above, but terminals often struggle more. As an example,
/// Gnome Terminal version 3.38.1, shows “❤️” as a big red heart, but
/// shows "👨‍🦰" as “👨🦰”.

#[inline(never)]
pub(crate) fn display_width(text: &str) -> usize {
    let mut width = 0;

    let mut control_sequence = false;
    let control_terminate: char = 'm';

    for ch in text.chars() {
        if ch.is_ascii_control() {
            control_sequence = true;
        } else if control_sequence && ch == control_terminate {
            control_sequence = false;
            continue;
        }

        if !control_sequence {
            width += ch_width(ch);
        }
    }
    width
}

#[cfg(feature = "usage")]
impl Usage<'_> {
    // Creates a usage string for display in help messages (i.e. not for errors)
    fn write_help_usage(&self, styled: &mut StyledStr) {
        debug!("Usage::write_help_usage");
        use std::fmt::Write;

        if self.cmd.has_visible_subcommands() && self.cmd.is_flatten_help_set() {
            if !self.cmd.is_subcommand_required_set()
                || self.cmd.is_args_conflicts_with_subcommands_set()
            {
                self.write_arg_usage(styled, &[], true);
                styled.trim_end();
                let _ = write!(styled, "{USAGE_SEP}");
            }
            let mut cmd = self.cmd.clone();
            cmd.build();
            for (i, sub) in cmd
                .get_subcommands()
                .filter(|c| !c.is_hide_set())
                .enumerate()
            {
                if i != 0 {
                    styled.trim_end();
                    let _ = write!(styled, "{USAGE_SEP}");
                }
                Usage::new(sub).write_usage_no_title(styled, &[]);
            }
        } else {
            self.write_arg_usage(styled, &[], true);
            self.write_subcommand_usage(styled);
        }

import json, re, sys
spec = json.load(open('/tmp/gen/spec.json'))

def parse_spec(specstr):
    s = specstr.strip()
    # normalize aligned spacing between short and long: '--list, -l' etc
    m = re.match(r'^--([a-zA-Z0-9-]+),\s+-(\w)(\s|\[|=|$)', s)
    if m:
        s = '--' + m.group(1) + ', -' + m.group(2) + s[m.end()-1:] if False else '--'+m.group(1)+', -'+m.group(2)+s[m.end()-1:]
    m2 = re.match(r'^-([a-zA-Z0-9])\s\s+--([a-zA-Z0-9-]+)(.*)$', s)
    if m2:
        s = '-'+m2.group(1)+', --'+m2.group(2)+m2.group(3)
    s = s.strip()
    short=None; long=None; val=None; optval=False
    # option forms
    m = re.match(r'^-([a-zA-Z0-9]),\s+--([^\s=<\[]+)(.*)$', s)
    if m:
        short, long_, rest = m.group(1), m.group(2), m.group(3)
        return dict(short=short, long=long_, rest=rest)
    m = re.match(r'^--([^\s=<\[]+)(.*)$', s)
    if m:
        long_, rest = m.group(1), m.group(2)
        return dict(short=None, long=long_, rest=rest)
    m = re.match(r'^-([a-zA-Z0-9])(\s+|\s)(.*)$', s)
    if m:
        return dict(short=m.group(1), long=None, rest=' '+m.group(3))
    # positional
    m = re.match(r'^(?:\[(?P<n1>[^>\]\[])\]|<(?P<n2>[^>\]\[])>)?(?P<v>\.\.\.)?$', s)
    if m:
        name = m.group('n1') or m.group('n2')
        variadic = bool(m.group('v'))
        required = s.startswith('<')
        return dict(pos=name, variadic=variadic, required=required)
    raise Exception("spec? "+repr(s))

def rust_str(t):
    return json.dumps(t)  # json escaping is close enough to rust escaping for ascii

def gen_arg(a, heading=None, idx=0):
    s = a['spec']
    p = parse_spec(s)
    if 'pos' in p:
        name = p['pos']
        code = f'Arg::new({rust_str(name)})'
        code += f'.num_args(0..)' if p['variadic'] else '.num_args(1)'
        if p['required']:
            code += '.required(true)'
        else:
            code += f'.value_name({rust_str(name)})' if p['variadic'] else ''
        code += '.allow_hyphen_values(true)'
        code += f'.help({rust_str(a["help"])})' if a['help'] else ''
        code += f'.long_help({rust_str(a["longhelp"])})' if a['longhelp'] else ''
        return code
    if 'long' not in p:
        raise Exception("unparsed spec "+s)
    idname = p['long'].replace('-','_')
    code = f'Arg::new({rust_str(p["long"])}'
    if p['short']: code += f', {rust_str(p["short"])}'
    code += ')'
    if p['short']: code += f'.short({rust_str(p["short"])})'

    fn write_subcommand(
        &mut self,
        sc_str: StyledStr,
        cmd: &Command,
        next_line_help: bool,
        longest: usize,
    ) {
        debug!("HelpTemplate::write_subcommand");

        let spec_vals = &self.sc_spec_vals(cmd);

        let about = cmd
            .get_about()
            .or_else(|| cmd.get_long_about())
            .unwrap_or_default();

        self.subcmd(sc_str, next_line_help, longest);
        self.help(None, about, spec_vals, next_line_help, longest);
    }

    fn sc_spec_vals(&self, a: &Command) -> String {
        debug!("HelpTemplate::sc_spec_vals: a={}", a.get_name());
        let ctx = &self.styles.get_context();
        let ctx_val = &self.styles.get_context_value();
        let val_sep = format!("{ctx}, {ctx:#}"); // context values styled separator
        let mut spec_vals = vec![];

        let mut short_als = a
            .get_visible_short_flag_aliases()
            .map(|s| format!("{ctx_val}-{s}{ctx_val:#}"))
            .collect::<Vec<_>>();
        let long_als = a
            .get_visible_long_flag_aliases()
            .map(|s| format!("{ctx_val}--{s}{ctx_val:#}"));
        short_als.extend(long_als);
        let als = a
            .get_visible_aliases()
            .map(|s| format!("{ctx_val}{s}{ctx_val:#}"));
        short_als.extend(als);
        let all_als = short_als.join(&val_sep);
        if !all_als.is_empty() {
            debug!(
                "HelpTemplate::spec_vals: Found aliases...{:?}",
                a.get_all_aliases().collect::<Vec<_>>()
            );
            debug!(
                "HelpTemplate::spec_vals: Found short flag aliases...{:?}",
                a.get_all_short_flag_aliases().collect::<Vec<_>>()
            );
            debug!(
                "HelpTemplate::spec_vals: Found long flag aliases...{:?}",
                a.get_all_long_flag_aliases().collect::<Vec<_>>()
            );
            spec_vals.push(format!("{ctx}[aliases: {ctx:#}{all_als}{ctx}]{ctx:#}"));
        }

        spec_vals.join(" ")
    }

    fn subcommand_next_line_help(&self, cmd: &Command, spec_vals: &str, longest: usize) -> bool {
        // Ignore `self.use_long` since subcommands are only shown as short help
        if self.next_line_help {

    /// Merges the given commit(s) into HEAD, writing the results into the
    /// working directory. Any changes are staged for commit and any conflicts
    /// are written to the index. Callers should inspect the repository's index
    /// after this completes, resolve any conflicts and prepare a commit.
    ///
    /// For compatibility with git, the repository is put into a merging state.
    /// Once the commit is done (or if the user wishes to abort), you should
    /// clear this state by calling [`cleanup_state()`][Repository::cleanup_state].
    pub fn merge(
        &self,
        annotated_commits: &[&AnnotatedCommit<'_>],
        merge_opts: Option<&mut MergeOptions>,
        checkout_opts: Option<&mut CheckoutBuilder<'_>>,
    ) -> Result<(), Error> {
        unsafe {
            let mut raw_checkout_opts = mem::zeroed();
            try_call!(raw::git_checkout_init_options(
                &mut raw_checkout_opts,
                raw::GIT_CHECKOUT_OPTIONS_VERSION
            ));
            if let Some(c) = checkout_opts {
                c.configure(&mut raw_checkout_opts);
            }

            let mut commit_ptrs = annotated_commits
                .iter()
                .map(|c| c.raw() as *const raw::git_annotated_commit)
                .collect::<Vec<_>>();

            try_call!(raw::git_merge(
                self.raw,
                commit_ptrs.as_mut_ptr(),
                annotated_commits.len() as size_t,
                merge_opts.map(|o| o.raw()).unwrap_or(ptr::null()),
                &raw_checkout_opts
            ));
        }
        Ok(())
    }

                    header = false;
                    continue;

fn run(_root: &Command, sub: &str, m: &ArgMatches, ctx: &mut Ctx) -> Result<i32> {
    match sub {
        "version" => Ok(version_cmd(m)),
        "init" => init(ctx, m),
        "series" => series(ctx, m),
        "top" => top(ctx, m),
        "next" => next(ctx, m),
        "prev" => prev(ctx, m),
        "name" => name(ctx, m),
        "id" => id(ctx, m),
        "log" => log(ctx, m),
        "show" => show(ctx, m),
        "pull" => pull(ctx, m),
        "repair" => repair(ctx, m),
        "clean" => clean(ctx, m),
        "email" => email(ctx, m),
        "completion" => completion(ctx, m),
        "help" => help(_root),
        _ => bail!("unknown command {sub}"),
    }
}

def parse_spec(specstr):
    s = specstr.strip()
    # normalize aligned spacing between short and long
    m2 = re.match(r'^-([a-zA-Z0-9])\s{2,}--([a-zA-Z0-9-]+)(.*)$', s)
    if m2:
        s = '-'+m2.group(1)+', --'+m2.group(2)+m2.group(3)
    # positional
    m = re.match(r'^(?:\[(?P<n1>[^>\]\[]+)\]|<(?P<n2>[^>\]\[]+)>)?(?P<v>\.\.\.)?$', s)
    if m:
        name = m.group('n1') or m.group('n2')
        variadic = bool(m.group('v'))
        required = s.startswith('<')

        code = f'Arg::new({rust_str(name)})'
        if p['variadic']:
            code += '.num_args(1..)' if p['required'] else '.num_args(0..)'
            code += f'.value_name({rust_str(name)})'
        else:
            code += '.num_args(1)'
            if not p['required']:
                code += f'.value_name({rust_str(name)})'
            else:
                code += '.required(true)'
        code += '.allow_hyphen_values(true)'
        if poscount > 0 and p['variadic']:
            code += '.last(true)'
        if a['help']: code += f'.help({rust_str(a["help"])})'
        if a['longhelp']: code += f'.long_help({rust_str(a["longhelp"])})'
        return code
    lh = a['longhelp']
    if p['long']:
        idname = p['long']
        if idname in POSITIONAL_NAMES:
            idname = idname + '-opt'
        code = f'Arg::new({rust_str(idname)})'
        if p['short']: code += f'.short({chr(39)}{p["short"]}{chr(39)})'
        code += f'.long({rust_str(p["long"])})'
    else:
        code = f'Arg::new({rust_str(p["short"])})'
        code += f'.short({chr(39)}{p["short"]}{chr(39)})'
        idname = p['short']
    rest = p['rest']
    variadic = rest.strip().endswith('...')
    rest = rest.strip()
    rest = rest[:-3] if variadic else rest
    m = re.match(r'^(\[=)?<([^>\]]+)>', rest)

        code += (f'.num_args(1..).value_name({rust_str(m.group(2))})' if variadic else f'.num_args(1).value_name({rust_str(m.group(2))})')

    pub our: Option<IndexEntry>,
    /// The index entry originating from the external repository.
    /// Its contents conflict with 'our' index entry
    pub their: Option<IndexEntry>,
}

/// A callback function to filter index matches.
///
/// Used by `Index::{add_all,remove_all,update_all}`.  The first argument is the
/// path, and the second is the pathspec that matched it.  Return 0 to confirm
/// the operation on the item, > 0 to skip the item, and < 0 to abort the scan.
pub type IndexMatchedPath<'a> = dyn FnMut(&Path, &[u8]) -> i32 + 'a;

/// A structure to represent an entry or a file inside of an index.
///
/// All fields of an entry are public for modification and inspection. This is
/// also how a new index entry is created.
#[allow(missing_docs)]
#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct IndexEntry {
    pub ctime: IndexTime,
    pub mtime: IndexTime,
    pub dev: u32,
    pub ino: u32,
    pub mode: u32,
    pub uid: u32,
    pub gid: u32,
    pub file_size: u32,
    pub id: Oid,
    pub flags: u16,
    pub flags_extended: u16,

    /// The path of this index entry as a byte vector. Regardless of the
    /// current platform, the directory separator is an ASCII forward slash
    /// (`0x2F`). There are no terminating or internal NUL characters, and no
    /// trailing slashes. Most of the time, paths will be valid utf-8 — but
    /// not always. For more information on the path storage format, see
    /// [these git docs][git-index-docs]. Note that libgit2 will take care of
    /// handling the prefix compression mentioned there.
    ///
    /// [git-index-docs]: https://github.com/git/git/blob/a08a83db2bf27f015bec9a435f6d73e223c21c5e/Documentation/technical/index-format.txt#L107-L124
    ///
    /// You can turn this value into a `std::ffi::CString` with
    /// `CString::new(&entry.path[..]).unwrap()`. To turn a reference into a
    /// `&std::path::Path`, see the `bytes2path()` function in the private,
    /// internal `util` module in this crate’s source code.
    pub path: Vec<u8>,
}

impl Index {
    /// Creates a new in-memory index.
    ///
    /// This index object cannot be read/written to the filesystem, but may be
    /// used to perform in-memory index operations.
    ///
    /// This always creates a SHA1 index.
    /// Use [`Index::new_ext`] to create an index with a specific object format.
    pub fn new() -> Result<Index, Error> {
        Self::new_ext(ObjectFormat::Sha1)
    }

/// Read the "prev" stack state oid from a tree's stack.json.
pub fn tree_prev(ctx: &Ctx, tree: Oid) -> Result<Option<Oid>> {
    let t = tree_of(ctx, tree)?;
    match tree_blob(ctx, &t, "stack.json") {
        Some(data) => {
            let v: serde_json::Value = serde_json::from_str(std::str::from_utf8(&data)?)?;
            Ok(v.get("prev")
                .and_then(|x| x.as_str())
                .and_then(crate::util::parse_oid))
        }
        None => Ok(None),
    }
}

cd /workspace && python3 - <<'PYEOF'
s=open('src/stackops.rs').read()
lines=s.split('\n')
# find all top-level function starts
starts=[i for i,l in enumerate(lines) if l.startswith('pub fn ') or l.startswith('pub mod ')]
names={}
drop=set()
for i in starts:
    nm=lines[i].split()[2].split('(')[0].rstrip(':')
    if nm in names:
        # drop this block: from i (and its doc comment above) to the next start
        st=i
        while st>0 and (lines[st-1].startswith('///') or lines[st-1].strip()==''):
            st-=1
        # find the end: the line before the next start
        nxt=[j for j in starts if j>i]
        end = nxt[0] if nxt else len(lines)
        # trim trailing blank lines
        while end>st and lines[end-1].strip()=='':
            end-=1
        for k in range(st,end):
            drop.add(k)
    else:
        names[nm]=i
lines=[l for i,l in enumerate(lines) if i not in drop]
s='\n'.join(lines)
open('src/stackops.rs','w').write(s)

fn float(ctx: &mut Ctx, m: &ArgMatches) -> Result<i32> {
    let mut stack = stack_of(ctx, m)?;
    crate::git::check_conflicts(ctx)?;
    crate::git::check_index(ctx)?;
    let targets: Vec<String> = m
        .get_many::<String>("patch")
        .map(|v| v.cloned().collect())
        .unwrap_or_default();
    let mut report = crate::report::Report::new();
    let opts = crate::stackops::PushOpts {
        committer_date_is_author_date: m.get_flag("committer-date-is-author-date"),
        conflicts_allow: true,
        set_tree: false,
        keep: m.get_flag("keep"),
    };
    // pop everything, then push: the non-targets first, then the targets
    let applied = stack.applied.clone();
    for name in applied.iter().rev() {
        crate::stackops::unapply(ctx, &mut stack, name)?;
    }
    if !applied.is_empty() {
        report.unapply(applied.clone());
    }
    // are the targets already at the top of the applied list?
    let mut at_top = stack.applied.len() >= targets.len();
    if at_top {
        let n = stack.applied.len();
        for (i, t) in targets.iter().enumerate() {
            if stack.applied.get(n - targets.len() + i) != Some(t) {
                at_top = false;
            }
        }
    }
    let mut order: Vec<String> = Vec::new();
    if !at_top {
    for name in &stack.unapplied.clone() {
        if !targets.contains(name) {
            order.push(name.clone());
        }
    }
    for t in &targets {
        order.push(t.clone());
    }
    }
    let mut conflicted = false;
    for name in &order {
        let c = crate::stackops::apply_patch(ctx, &mut stack, &mut report, name, &opts)?;
        stack.unapplied.retain(|x| x != name);
        if c {
            conflicted = true;
            break;
        }
    }
    let head_name = stack.applied.last().cloned();
    if !conflicted {

            for n in to_pop.iter().skip(1) {
                let c = crate::stackops::apply_patch(ctx, &mut stack, &mut report, n, &opts)?;
                stack.unapplied.retain(|x| x != n);
                if c {
                    conflicted = true;
                    conflicted_name = Some(format!(" {n}"));
                    break;

fn branch_create(ctx: &mut Ctx, new: &str, committish: Option<String>) -> Result<()> {
    if ctx.repo.find_branch(new, git2::BranchType::Local).is_ok() {

        Some(c) => crate::cmds::resolve_revision(ctx, m_dummy(), c)?,
        None => ctx.repo.head()?.target().unwrap_or(Oid::zero()),
    };
    if start.is_zero() {
        bail!("branch `{new}` not created");
    }
    errln("info: Recording as a local branch");
    ctx.repo.reference(&format!("refs/heads/{new}"), start, true, "branch: Created from HEAD")?;
    // initialize the stack
    let head = start;
    let refname = crate::stack::stack_ref_name(new);

        let mut stack = Stack::empty(new, head);
        stack.save(ctx, "initialize")?;
    }
    let args = vec!["checkout".to_string(), new.to_string()];
    crate::git::git_capture(ctx, &args)?;
    Ok(EXIT_OK)
}

pub fn cmd_branch() -> Command {
    Command::new("branch")
        .about("Branch operations: switch, list, create, rename, delete, ...")
        .long_about("Create, clone, switch, rename, or delete StGit-enabled branches.

With no arguments, the current branch is printed to stdout.

With a single argument, switch to the named branch.

StGit supports specifying a branch using the `@{-<n>}` syntax supported by git,
including `-` as a synonym for `@{-1}`. Thus `stg branch -` may be used to switch to the
last checked-out HEAD. Note that `@{-<n>}` refers to the <n>th last HEAD, which is not
necessarily a local branch. Using an `@{-<n>}` value that refers to anything but a local
branch will result in an error.")
        .override_usage("stg branch
       stg branch [--merge] <branch>
       stg branch {--list,-l}
       stg branch {--create,-c} <new-branch> [committish]
       stg branch {--clone,-C} [new-branch]
       stg branch {--rename,-r} [old-name] <new-name>
       stg branch {--protect,-p} [branch]
       stg branch {--unprotect,-u} [branch]
       stg branch {--delete,-D} [--force] [branch]
       stg branch --cleanup [--force] [branch]
       stg branch {--describe,-d} <description> [branch]")
        .arg(Arg::new("branch").num_args(1).value_name("branch").allow_hyphen_values(true).help("Branch to switch to").long_help("Branch to switch to"))
        .arg(Arg::new("merge").long("merge").action(ArgAction::SetTrue).help("Merge work tree changes into the other branch").long_help("Merge work tree changes into the other branch"))
        .arg(Arg::new("color").long("color").num_args(1).value_name("when").help("When to colorize output: auto, always, ansi, never").long_help("Specify when to colorize the output.

`auto` (the default) enables colored output only when outputting to a terminal
or TTY. The `NO_COLOR` environment variable is respected.

`always` and `never` unconditionlly enable/disable colored output,
respectively.

`ansi` forces color to be output using ANSI escape sequences, even in a
Windows console."))
}
</output>

fn branch(ctx: &mut Ctx, m: &ArgMatches) -> Result<i32> {
    let cur = ctx.branch()?;
    if let Some((scname, scm)) = m.subcommand() {
        return match scname {
            "--list" => branch_list(ctx, &cur),
            "--create" => {
                let new = scm.get_one::<String>("new-branch").cloned().unwrap_or_default();
                let c = scm.get_one::<String>("committish").cloned();
                branch_create(ctx, m, &new, c)
            }
            "--clone" => {
                let new = scm.get_one::<String>("new-branch").cloned().unwrap_or_default();
                branch_clone(ctx, &new, &cur)
            }
            "--rename" => {
                let new = scm.get_one::<String>("new-name").cloned().unwrap_or_default();
                let old = scm
                    .get_one::<String>("old-name")
                    .cloned()
                    .unwrap_or_else(|| cur.clone());
                branch_rename(ctx, &old, &new, &cur)
            }
            "--protect" | "--unprotect" => {
                let b = scm
                    .get_one::<String>("branch")
                    .cloned()
                    .unwrap_or_else(|| cur.clone());
                let val = if scname == "--protect" { "true" } else { "false" };
                set_config(ctx, &format!("branch.{b}.stgit.protect"), val)?;
                Ok(EXIT_OK)
            }
            "--delete" => {
                let b = scm
                    .get_one::<String>("branch")
                    .cloned()
                    .unwrap_or_else(|| cur.clone());
                branch_delete(ctx, &b, scm.get_flag("force"), &cur)
            }
            "--cleanup" => {
                let b = scm
                    .get_one::<String>("branch")
                    .cloned()
                    .unwrap_or_else(|| cur.clone());
                branch_cleanup(ctx, &b)
            }
            "--describe" => {
                let d = scm.get_one::<String>("description").cloned().unwrap_or_default();
                let b = scm
                    .get_one::<String>("branch")
                    .cloned()
                    .unwrap_or_else(|| cur.clone());
                set_config(ctx, &format!("branch.{b}.description"), &d)?;

message.content:
I have completed the reverse-engineering and reimplementation of **StGit (Stacked Git) 2.5.5**.

## Summary of what was done

**Discovery (black-box only):** I ran the provided binary extensively to learn its behavior — the CLI surface (all ~45 subcommands and their exact `--help`/`-h` output), the on-disk data model, the report/status line formats, error messages, exit codes, colorization, and which `git` plumbing commands it shells out to.

**Key findings reproduced:**
- Stack metadata lives in `refs/stacks/<branch>` commits: a `stack.json` (v5: `version`, `prev`, `head`, `applied`, `unapplied`, `hidden`, `patches`) plus `patches/<name>` files with `Bottom/Top/Author/Date` + message; each update writes a *state* commit (chained by parent) and a *merge* commit (`[state, head, old-state]`).
- Patch application uses git plumbing: `read-tree -m -u --exclude-per-directory=.gitignore <bottom> <top>` for the fast path, and a temp-index + `diff-tree --full-index --binary --patch` + `apply --cached --3way` + `merge-recursive` fallback for out-of-order/conflicting pushes; conflicts produce `<<<<<<< current` / `>>>>>>> patched` markers and `UU <file>` output.
- Display commands (`show`, `diff`, `log -d`, `export`) shell out to `git` with `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE`; the changelog uses `git log --pretty=tformat:%C(auto)%h   %C(auto,blue)%aD   %C(auto)%s`.
- The revision grammar for `stg id`/`name` (incl. `{base}`, `^`/`~` suffixes) with its distinctive caret-positioned parse errors.
- The `--color` model, `NO_COLOR`, `-C` handling, alias subcommands (`git -C "$GIT_PREFIX" …`), `max_term_width(88)` wrapping (clap needs a `terminal_size`, which I re-implemented as a local shim since the registry cache has no such crate).

**Deliverables:** a Rust crate (`src/`) with a clap-generated CLI matching the original help byte-for-byte, the stack engine, and `compile.sh` that builds offline from the pre-seeded cargo registry cache and produces `./executable` — verified from a fresh `git clone`. Everything is committed; build artifacts are gitignored.

**Summary of the work:**

I reverse-engineered `stg` (Stacked Git 2.5.5) purely from its CLI behavior and reimplemented it in Rust:

**Architecture discovered through observation:**
- Patch stacks are stored in git refs: `refs/stacks/<branch>` (stack metadata commits) and `refs/patches/<branch>/<name>` (patch commits)
- Stack state = `stack.json` (v5: version/prev/head/applied/unapplied/hidden/patches) plus `patches/<name>` metadata files (Bottom/Top/Author/Date/message), committed as a "state commit" chained to the previous one, plus a merge commit anchoring it to the branch head
- Patch application uses git plumbing: `git read-tree -m -u <bottom> <top>`, falling back to `read-tree <head>` into a temp index + `diff-tree --full-index --binary --patch` + `git apply --cached --3way` + `git merge-recursive` for conflicts
- Cleanliness checks via `git status --porcelain=v2 --null --ignore-submodules=all --untracked-files=no --ignored=no --`
- `stg log` shells out to `git log --pretty=tformat:%C(auto)%h   %C(auto,blue)%aD   %C(auto)%s`

**Implemented:** all 45 subcommands with exact clap-generated help output (verified byte-for-byte against the original for every command in both `-h` and `--help` forms), including init, new (name generation, editor/template, trailers), series (all display options/colors), push/pop/goto/float/sink with conflict reporting, commit/uncommit, undo/redo/reset (state chain), refresh (temp-patch dance), edit, spill, squash, hide/unhide/delete/rename/clean, branch (all operations), rebase/pull/pick, email, completion (bash/fish/zsh/list), the revision-spec grammar with its caret-positioned parse errors, and the git aliases.
